newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-New Inchcape faces interim test.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-New Inchcape faces interim test.

text.p: Inchcape Plc has certainly tested the patience of its investors in the last 18 months -- and on Monday analysts expect its new management will find themselves under pressure to deliver.
The international distribution group put in a dire financial performance in 1995, undermined by weak currencies, car markets and cost controls, and new managers have promised a turnaround.

In March new chairman Sir Colin Marshall and chief executive Philip Cushing had to cut 1995's full-year dividend by a third and pledged they would reshape the group this year by divesting its two biggest service units. Now investors want some results.
Analysts hope that Inchcape's first half financial report on Monday will show the all-important early signs of change.

"There is a real need for a decisive shift in performance to bring Inchcape back into favour," said one analyst, who asked not to be named. But he warned that market fundamentals remained uncertain and could delay a recovery until later this year.

Nevertheless, analysts polled by Reuters saw the company reporting a barely changed pretax profit of 80.48 million stg, versus 83.0 million in the same period last year. The range of forecasts polled by Reuters spanned from 73 to 88 million.
Most analysts also expect another lower dividend payout.

While Inchcape paid out 6.0 pence at the interim stage last year it cut its final payout to 4.0 pence for a full-year total of 10.0 pence. Analysts do not yet expect to see a return to 6.0 pence at the halfway, and most expected another 4.0p this time. While they can accept that the payout will need some time to recover, analysts are eager to see a rebound in the business.

"Profitability from motors will be a big area of focus," said analyst Heather Grundy at Liverpool brokerage Tilney & Co, adding she would be looking for a reversal of the trend in Inchcape's operating margins from motors, which plunged in 1995.
News of insurance arm Bain Hogg's float is also expected.
After months of rumours and media speculation, analysts said, it was almost inevitable that Monday would see the announcement of a timetable for Bain Hogg's flotation.

If the board is still behind this form of divestment rather than a last-minute trade sale, then one analyst said that an impact day in mid-October looked likely with the company eyeing a start of trade for the shares in the early part of November.

Even if the long silence on disposals is broken, analysts are divided on the likely impact on Inchcape's depressed share price. Some hope for a break out above 310 pence, a resistance level for the share established since April.
Others warn that, without the support of the dividend at the previous, generous level, the shares could fall severely if the earnings news is perceived as disappointing.
"We saw a floor of 260p earlier this summer and it may not take very much bad news to send it there again," one said.
Just a year ago the shares were around 350p, having slipped steadily since autumn 1994 when they stood nearer 460p.
The share price edged up 2.0 p to 304-1/2p by 1230 GMT on Friday in reasonable volume.
